Part 1 assumed that the tools were already installed. This part shows how to
install them, and explains why this is harder than it sounds.

::: {.callout-note}
## Most commands on this page are not executed

The examples on this page install software, unlike those in Part 1. They need
the internet, they take minutes, and several of them use an installer that you
do not have yet. So they are shown, but not run automatically. The version
numbers are only examples.
:::

# The problem

You install a tool, and it works. Six months later you install a second tool
for another project, and the first tool stops working.

This is not bad luck. Tools are built on other tools: libraries, interpreters,
system packages. Two programs can need **different versions of the same
dependency**, and these versions may not work together. If you install one
version for the whole computer, it replaces the version that the other program
needed.

A package manager must do three things to solve this:

1. **Install software** without you compiling anything.
2. **Resolve dependencies:** find a set of versions that fits every
   requirement at once, or say clearly that no such set exists.
3. **Keep projects separate**, so that the tools of one project cannot break
   the tools of another.

An **environment** (dt. *Umgebung*) does the third job. It is a separate set of
tools that belongs to one project. Two environments on the same computer can
contain different versions of the same program, and they do not affect each
other.

::: {.callout-important}
## The other reason environments matter

An environment can be written down. If a file records the exact versions that
produced a result, someone else can recreate the environment and get the same
result. That someone can also be you, next year.

Without such a file, you cannot find out why a result differs on another
computer. This is the strongest reason to use environments at all, and it is
why the file is more important than the tool.
:::

# pixi

**This material recommends [pixi](https://pixi.sh).** pixi is a package manager
that uses the same package repositories as the older tools, so it can install
the same software. But it is organised around the *project*, not around your
computer.

## Installing pixi

```{.bash .no-run}
curl -fsSL https://pixi.sh/install.sh | bash
```

Close the terminal, open a new one, and check that pixi is installed:

```{.bash .no-run}
pixi --version
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## About `curl … | bash`

You have just downloaded a script and run it without reading it. Be aware of
this. Many installers work this way, but a harmful script can also get onto
your computer this way. So do this only for projects that you trust, and use
the official website, not a link that someone sent you.
:::

## Starting a project

```{.bash .no-run}
pixi init myproject
cd myproject
```

This creates a directory with a file `pixi.toml` in it. Now add a tool:

```{.bash .no-run}
pixi add python
```

Run a command inside the environment of the project:

```{.bash .no-run}
pixi run python --version
```

The important point: **you did not "activate" anything.** `pixi run` uses the
tools of this project because you are in the directory of this project. If you
move to another project, the same command uses the tools of that project.

## The two files

| file | what it is | commit it? |
|---|---|---|
| `pixi.toml` | what you *asked for* — "python, and samtools" | **yes** |
| `pixi.lock` | what you actually *got* — every package, exact version, checksum | **yes** |

The lock file makes the environment reproducible. `pixi.toml` says "a recent
python". `pixi.lock` says exactly which version, for every platform that the
project supports. If someone clones your project and runs:

```{.bash .no-run}
pixi install
```

they get exactly what you had, not only something similar. **Commit both
files.** If you delete the lock file to "fix" a problem, you delete the only
record of the versions that worked.

## Channels

Packages come from **channels**: repositories of software that is already
built. Two channels are important here:

- **conda-forge** — general software: Python, R, compilers, libraries.
- **bioconda** — tools for the life sciences.

Each project lists its channels in its own `pixi.toml`. So the project does not
depend on how your computer is configured:

```toml
[workspace]
channels = ["conda-forge", "bioconda"]
platforms = ["linux-64"]
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## bioconda does not build for Windows

Most life-science tools have no Windows packages. This will not change, and it
is why Part 1 tells Windows users to install WSL2. Inside WSL2 you are on
`linux-64`, and everything works.

macOS is supported, but not for every tool. Some tools have no version for Apple
Silicon, and an environment that installs on Linux may not install on a Mac.
:::

# conda and mamba

You will see these tools. Most documentation, most methods sections in papers
and most older lab protocols are written for **conda**. So you should know what
conda and mamba are, even though this material does not recommend them for new
work.

| | |
|---|---|
| **conda** | the original tool. Same channels, same packages. Resolving dependencies could be extremely slow: minutes to hours for a large environment. |
| **mamba** | a much faster new version of the part of conda that resolves dependencies. For a long time, the usual advice was "install conda, then use mamba instead". |
| **pixi** | organised around the project, and it always writes a lock file. Again the same packages. |

Today, conda is much faster than it was, because it now uses the same method as
mamba. So the old advice "conda is too slow to use" is out of date. Speed is not
the reason to prefer pixi.

## Translating between them

If you find instructions for conda, this table shows the pixi equivalents:

| conda / mamba | pixi |
|---|---|
| `conda create -n myenv` | `pixi init myproject` |
| `conda activate myenv` | *(nothing — be in the directory)* |
| `conda install samtools` | `pixi add samtools` |
| `conda deactivate` | *(nothing)* |
| `conda env export > env.yml` | *(already done — `pixi.lock`)* |
| `conda env create -f env.yml` | `pixi install` |

## Why this material recommends pixi

There are three concrete differences. They are not a matter of taste:

1. **The lock file is always there.** conda can write one, but only with extra
   tools and extra effort. pixi writes one every time, so your environment is
   reproducible without any extra work.
2. **The environment belongs to the project, not to you.** You do not need to
   manage a list of environments, and you cannot forget which one is active. If
   you are in the directory, you have the right tools.
3. **You cannot forget to activate anything.** The most common problem with
   conda is to run a command in the wrong environment. Then you get a confusing
   error, or even worse, a wrong result from an older version.

::: {.callout-note}
## None of this makes conda wrong

conda is used everywhere, it works, and you will need to read instructions for
it. If you join a group that uses conda, use conda. The concepts are the same in
both tools: channels, environments, resolving dependencies, and an environment
that is written down in a file.
:::

# When it goes wrong

**"Solving environment" takes a very long time, then fails.** This means that
no combination of versions fits everything you asked for. Usually one fixed
version is the problem. Allow more versions, or install the difficult tool in a
separate project. A second environment costs little; a broken environment costs
a lot.

**The tool installs but does not run.** Often the package was built for another
processor type: for example, a package for `linux-64` on an Apple Silicon Mac,
or the other way round. Check which platforms the project lists.

**It works for you but not for a colleague.** The lock file exists to prevent
this. If your colleague uses the lock file and the results still differ, the
difference is outside the environment: the operating system, or a tool that was
installed in another way.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Never install project tools system-wide

`sudo apt install <a scientific tool>` installs the tool outside every
environment. There, no file records it, and nobody can reproduce it. It is also
often an old version. Keep the tools of a project in the project.
:::
